title: Overfitting seen first-hand
objectives: Watch the training loss fall while the dev loss rises, and choose a model by its dev loss.

screens.title: Bigger and fewer
screens.prose: Train a much larger network, a hidden layer of 300 instead of 100, on only the first 1,000 training names: 7,226 rows instead of 182,531. Same start, same batches, 20,000 steps.
screens.question: What do you expect its dev loss to do over the 20,000 steps?

options.text: Fall at first, then rise as it learns the 1,000 names by heart
Keep falling, since it is bigger
options.why: Bigger helps only while there is enough data; 7,226 rows run out fast.

options.text: Stay at the start, since it has too little data
options.why: It learns at first, from what the 1,000 names share with the rest.

hints.text: What can about 18,000 weights do with 7,226 rows?

feedback.correct: Fall, then rise: training on few names, it starts fitting their quirks.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what a big model does with few examples.

byKey.fall: You expected size to win. With few names a big model fits their quirks, and the dev loss turns up.

explain.text: At first the network learns what all names share, and the dev loss falls. Then, with 300 hidden units and only 7,226 rows, it starts fitting these particular names, and the dev loss climbs.

screens.title: The recorded run
screens.prose: Reveal the run: training loss solid, dev loss dashed, the bigram’s dev loss as a reference line.

state.caption: Hidden layer of 300 on the first 1,000 training names (7,226 rows): losses every 250 steps.

screens.question: At about which step is the dev loss least?

options.why: By then the dev loss is 3.0981, its worst.
It falls at first; its lowest point is at step 2,000.
By then dev is 2.8568 and rising.

hints.text: Reveal the first tenth of the run.

feedback.correct: About step 2,000, where dev is 2.4568; after that it trends upward.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the lowest point of the dashed line.

explain.text: Dev falls to 2.4568 at step 2,000, then climbs to 3.0981 while the training loss keeps falling to 1.5534. It never gets below the bigram’s 2.4514.

screens.title: Overfitting
screens.prose: Name it: **overfitting** is learning the training names rather than the pattern of names, seen as a training loss that keeps falling while the dev loss rises. The cure the course uses first is to choose the model by its dev loss.

state.caption: The overfitting run at five recorded steps.

screens.question: What is the gap between dev and train at step 20,000? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: $1.5447$ nats: the network has learned its 1,000 names, not names.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract train from dev at step 20,000.

byKey.start: That is the gap at step 1,000.

explain.text: At step 20,000 train is 1.5534 and dev 3.0981, a gap of 1.5447 nats. At step 1,000 it was only 0.1651.

screens.title: Reading the gap
screens.prose: The gap is the dev loss minus the training loss at each recorded step.

state.caption: The overfitting run at five recorded steps.

screens.question: What is the gap at step 5,000? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: $0.7407$: the gap widens with every recorded step.

byKey.sum: You added the losses; the gap is their difference.

explain.text: The gap grows from 0.1651 at step 1,000 to 0.7407 at 5,000 and 1.5447 at 20,000. A widening gap with a falling training loss is the signature of overfitting.

screens.title: With all the names
screens.prose: The course MLP (hidden 100, all 182,531 rows) ends at 2.1356 on train and 2.1609 on dev after 40,000 steps.

state.caption: The overfitting run at five recorded steps.

screens.question: Why is its gap so much smaller than the overfitting run’s?

options.text: Far more data for its size

options.why: It trained for twice as many steps, 40,000.
Both use the same seeds; the difference is the data and the size.

hints.text: 182,531 rows for 6,097 weights against 7,226 rows for about 18,000.

feedback.correct: Plenty of data for its size: a gap of 0.0254 nats.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the data with the model’s size.

explain.text: With 182,531 rows and 6,097 weights the MLP cannot memorise its names, so train and dev stay 0.0254 apart. More data is the first cure for overfitting; weight decay and dropout come in `nn-train` level 3.

screens.title: Progress?
screens.prose: A learner watches the overfitting run’s training loss fall from 2.2935 at step 1,000 to 1.5534 at step 20,000 and reports a large improvement.

state.caption: The overfitting run at five recorded steps.

screens.question: What is wrong with the report?

options.text: Dev rose: it got worse on new names
Nothing: a lower loss is better
options.why: Lower training loss is better at fitting these names, not at modelling names.

options.text: The losses are in nats, not bits
options.why: The units are fine; the set is the problem.

feedback.correct: The dev loss rose: the model memorised, it did not improve.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the dev column.

byKey.ok: You read the falling training loss as progress. On names it never saw, the model got worse.

explain.text: Training loss measures fit to the 1,000 names; dev measures names the model has not seen. One fell by 0.74 while the other rose by 0.64, so the network was memorising. Judge progress on dev.

screens.title: Too small to overfit
screens.prose: The bigram has 729 numbers. Its train and dev losses are 2.4536 and 2.4514.

state.caption: The overfitting run at five recorded steps.

screens.question: Why does the bigram not overfit?

options.text: Too small to memorise the names

options.why: Without smoothing the train loss falls a little, but the counts still average thousands of pairs a row.
The test names give 2.4702; the sets are alike, and the model is the reason.

hints.text: How many numbers does it have per training row?

feedback.correct: Too few numbers to memorise: train and dev are about 0.002 apart.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare its size with the data.

explain.text: A row of counts averages thousands of pairs, so no single name can move it much. Small models underfit rather than overfit; big ones need data or care.

screens.title: best_checkpoint() and a short run
screens.prose: Write `best_checkpoint(dev_losses, steps)`: the step with the least dev loss, the earliest on a tie. Then write `fit_and_gap(train_words, dev_words, steps, seed)`: train from `course_init()` with `train_mlp` (step 0.1) and return the losses on the training and dev rows.
screens.question: Write `best_checkpoint` and `fit_and_gap`.

widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests: a planted list with a tie, the recorded overfitting run (80 checkpoints) and a single checkpoint. Then a short run of 200 steps on the first 200 training names: its training loss below 2.54 and the dev loss more than 0.1 above it. The last runs 5 steps on 30 names and compares both losses exactly, to 6 places. `build_dataset`, `course_init`, `train_mlp`, `full_loss`, `train` and `dev` are ready.

mutants.symptom: Keeps the later of two tied checkpoints.
Returns the position, not the step.
Scores the training rows twice, so no gap can show.
Trains on the dev names and scores the training names.

hints.text: Keep the position of the least dev loss, updating only on a strictly smaller value.
`fit_and_gap`: build both datasets, `p = train_mlp(course_init(), Xt, Yt, steps, 0.1, seed)`, then `full_loss` on each.

feedback.correct: Your choice and run match: step 2,000, and a gap opening after only 200 steps on 200 names.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: On a tie keep the earlier step: 200, not 400.

explain.text: On 200 names, 200 steps already give train 2.423 against dev 2.655. The best checkpoint of the long run is step 2,000; a run that saves weights there keeps the model that generalises best.

screens.title: Fifty stocks
screens.prose: A researcher tunes a trading rule with 40 parameters on 50 stocks until its backtest Sharpe ratio reaches 3. On the other 450 stocks of the index, over the same years, its Sharpe ratio is 0.2.
screens.question: What happened?

options.why: The years are the same; only the stocks differ.
Nothing marks them out; they are simply data the rule never fitted.

hints.text: Which stocks did the 40 parameters see?
Only the 50; the 450 are its dev set.

feedback.correct: Overfitting: 40 parameters fitted to 50 stocks, judged on the 450 it never saw.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare what the rule was fitted to with what it was judged on.

byKey.regime: Same years, different stocks: the change is in the data the rule saw, not the market.

explain.text: Like the network on 1,000 names, a rule with many parameters fitted to few stocks memorises them. The 450 held-out stocks play the dev set, and the drop from 3 to 0.2 is the gap.

ideas: A hidden layer of 300 on 1,000 names: train falls from 2.2935 to 1.5534 over 20,000 steps while dev rises from 2.4586 to 3.0981, never beating the bigram.
Overfitting is learning the training names, not the pattern; keep the checkpoint with the least dev loss, here step 2,000 (2.4568).
With all 182,531 rows the course MLP keeps train and dev close (2.1356 against 2.1609); the bigram is too small to overfit.

formula.name: Best checkpoint
formula.note: The earliest on a tie; never chosen on test.

summary.trap: Reading a falling training loss as progress while the dev loss rises.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep the least dev loss.

byKey.last: The last step has the most training, not the best dev loss.

explain.text: Dev is least at step 2,000 (2.47); after that the model fits its training names more and new names less.

quiz.prose: A model scores 1.80 on its training names and 2.60 on dev.
quiz.question: What does the gap of 0.80 nats suggest?

options.why: An underfitting model scores badly on both, with a small gap.
A small gap is normal; 0.80 nats is not.

explain.text: A training loss far below the dev loss means the model fits its own names much better than new ones.

quiz.question: Which change most directly reduces overfitting in the 1,000-name run?

options.why: More steps let it memorise further: the dev loss was rising.
A bigger model memorises more easily.

explain.text: With all 25,626 training names a network has far more data for its size: the course MLP, trained on all of them, keeps train and dev 0.025 apart.
